## 1. GLOBAL MACRO OVERVIEW

US economic momentum is weakening alongside a deteriorating inflation backdrop. First-quarter GDP was revised down to a 1.6% annualised rate from an initial 1.6% estimate (matching the revision), following anaemic 0.5% growth in Q4 2025. Consumer spending growth was revised lower to 1.4%, signalling that energy-price-driven inflation is increasingly squeezing household real income, which fell for a third consecutive month in April [Source: https://www.reuters.com/business/us-first-quarter-gdp-growth-revised-lower-16-pace-2026-05-28/]. Against this, April PCE inflation printed at 0.4% month-on-month (following a surge of 0.7% in March), with core PCE rising to 3.3% year-on-year — the fastest pace in three years — driven by a 5.5% monthly jump in gasoline and energy products [Source: https://www.reuters.com/business/us-pce-inflation-firmer-april-2026-05-28/].

The Federal Reserve is caught in a classic stagflationary bind. Under new Chair Kevin Warsh, the FOMC is unanimously holding rates at the current effective rate of 3.64% [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS], but the rhetoric is shifting hawkishly. Fed Governor Lisa Cook stated inflation is "clearly moving in the wrong direction" and signalled readiness to hike if prices don't ease, while CME FedWatch now prices a 40% probability of a rate hike by December [Source: https://www.reuters.com/business/feds-cook-says-she-is-prepared-raise-rates-if-inflation-doesnt-ease-2026-05-27/]. The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.48% and the 2-year at 4.00%, producing a still-inverted curve that reflects stagflationary anxiety [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10].

Equity markets are decoupling from the macro deterioration, powered almost entirely by AI and semiconductor momentum. Goldman Sachs raised its year-end S&P 500 target to 8,000, citing earnings growth as the primary driver, with the index up 9% year-to-date [Source: https://www.businessinsider.com/stock-market-outlook-sp500-8000-earnings-eps-goldman-sachs-forecast-2026-5]. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix surged 9% on Friday to join the $1 trillion market cap club following Micron's milestone earlier in the week, underpinning a powerful Asia-led chip rally [Source: https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-today-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-05-27-2026]. VIX has dipped to 15.71, consistent with subdued realised volatility despite the underlying macro risks [Source: Yahoo Finance (^VIX)].

The Iran war remains the dominant geopolitical and macro variable. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz since late February has disrupted global supply chains and energy flows, with 94% of chief economists surveyed expecting global inflation to rise as a result. Nearly 90% expect global growth to weaken over the coming year, though only 13% anticipate a full global recession [Source: https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article141428.html]. Today's price action suggests markets are pricing incremental peace deal probability, with Brent falling sharply on ceasefire framework hopes, even as the situation remains volatile following fresh US strikes earlier this week.

### Disputed

- [Report states Q1 GDP "revised down to a 1.6% annualised rate from an initial 1.6% estimate (matching the revision)"]: This is internally contradictory — the report acknowledges the revision matched the initial estimate, which means there was no downward revision. The Reuters source states growth "was not as strong as initially thought," suggesting the initial estimate was higher than 1.6%, but the data bundle does not provide the original first estimate to confirm the magnitude of the revision. The parenthetical "(matching the revision)" appears to be an editing error that contradicts the narrative framing.

- [Report states the FOMC "is unanimously holding rates"]: The news bundle indicates several FOMC members are openly debating potential hikes and some want to change policy statement language to reflect the next move could be a hike — suggesting the hold is not unanimous in spirit. More specifically, the CBS News article notes five members want to change the language on the policy statement. "Unanimously holding" overstates consensus.

- [Report states CPI YoY is implied to be in the 3.9% range via PCE framing, but the macro bundle shows CPI YoY at 3.95% as of April 1, 2026]: Minor inconsistency — the CBS News article cites an expected April PCE annual rate of 3.9%, but this is PCE, not CPI. The bundle's CPI figure of 3.95% is as of April 1 (likely March data), and the report does not separately cite CPI YoY, conflating PCE and CPI framing. The report should distinguish these two inflation measures more carefully.

- [Report describes the 2y/10y Treasury curve as "still-inverted"]: With the 10-year at 4.48% and the 2-year at 4.00%, the curve is positive (not inverted) by 48 basis points. This is a factual error — an inverted curve would require the 2-year yield to exceed the 10-year.

- [Report states gold is "rebounding firmly today (+1.39%) after hitting two-month lows below $4,400"]: The bundle's current gold price is $4,561.80 (+1.39%), which is consistent. However, the CNBC source states gold futures settled at $4,389.70 on Thursday, while the Mining.com source references a low "just above $4,400." The claim of lows "below $4,400" is supported by the CNBC futures settlement price ($4,377.10 intraday low cited) but conflicts with the Mining.com description of "just above $4,400." Minor inconsistency across sources, but the "below $4,400" claim is defensible from the CNBC data.

- [Report attributes NZD/USD surge to RBNZ governor signalling "earlier and steeper rate hikes" but the RBNZ actually *held* at 2.25% and the Kitco source notes the governor's comments about hikes — the WSJ source says the vote was split equally among 6 members (3-3), not the "governor signalled"]: The report correctly notes the hold and hawkish signal but attributes the NZD strength specifically to the governor's signalling in the Kitco forex article. The WSJ source confirms the split vote but does not attribute the hawkish signal specifically to the governor vs. the committee. This attribution is slightly imprecise but not materially wrong.
